## Overview

The Sumba, or Sumbanese, are an Austronesian ethnic group inhabiting Sumba Island in Indonesia. The island is divided into Southwest Sumba Regency, West Sumba Regency, Central Sumba Regency, and East Sumba Regency. They refer to themselves as *Tau Humba*. They describe a society that has retained much of its culture despite foreign influences and whose cultural expression includes customary ceremonies, traditional architecture, decorative carvings, textiles, jewelry, weapons, oral folklore, funerary rituals, horse races, bull sacrifices, and spear fighting.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Hinggi** — *Hinggi* are large body-covering sheets worn by men. They are made using weaving techniques, including ikat and pahikung, and their decorations express symbols connected with social and economic contexts, mythology, and Marapu belief.

**Lau** — *Lau* are women’s fabrics used as body coverings. Eastern Sumbese ceremonial dress includes several forms named according to weaving styles, including *lau kaworu*, *lau pahudu*, *lau lau mutikau*, and *pahudu kiku*.

**Hinggi kombu** — *Hinggi kombu* is worn on the hip and is regarded as the best of the named hinggi types. It is reinforced with a wide leather belt.

**Hinggi kaworu** — *Hinggi kaworu*, also called *hinggi raukadama*, is used as a complementary body covering. The sources rank it after hinggi kombu.

**Tiara** — *Tiara patang* is a headgear made from woven cloth. Its loops and knots form a crest whose position may carry symbolic meaning.

**Tiara pahudu** — *Tiara pahudu* is headgear made with the pahikung weaving technique.

**Lau pahudu kiku** — *Lau pahudu kiku* is a decorative fabric used as the lower part of the sarong, extending up to the chest.

**Motif vocabulary.** Human abstract or skull, prawn, chicken, snake, dragon, crocodile, horse, fish, turtle, squid, deer, bird, buffalo, three-colored flag, crown, lion.

### Clothing & dress

Sumba dress differs according to the importance of an event and its social setting. Special occasions include traditional celebrations, weddings, and death ceremonies, for which newly made components may be used, while old or worn clothing is generally used at home or for daily work. Men’s attire consists of headgear, body coverings, embellishments, and a bladed weapon. Two hinggi are used: hinggi kombu and hinggi kaworu. A tiara patang is tied around the head, and a kabeala is inserted on the left side of the belt. Traditionally men do not wear footwear, although footwear is commonly used, especially in the city.

Women’s ceremonial attire includes fabrics such as lau kaworu, lau pahudu, lau lau mutikau, and pahudu kiku. The sarong may cover the lower body up to the chest, while the shoulders are covered with a *taba huku* of the same color. The head dress includes a plain-colored tiara with *hiduhai* or *hai kara*. Women carry a *Kahidi Yutu* knife when leaving their residence or attending formal occasions.

### Architecture

The main settlement form is a village of houses built on hilltops and surrounded by dense thorny thickets as part of a defensive concept. Frame bamboo huts are built on poles, with walls overshadowing mats. Their thatched roofs have a complex structure designed to protect the houses from rain and sun and to provide natural ventilation. Marapu cultural expression includes traditional places of worship called *umaratu*, traditional architecture, and decorative carvings. By the twentieth century, Sumba people had built megalithic tombs, with Anakalang identified as the most famous location in the source.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

They mention stone carving, bamboo huts, mats, thatched roofs, leather belts, bladed weapons, knives, and woven textiles. Sumba people also keep cows, buffalo, chickens, sheep, and horses.

### Jewelry & body adornment

Men may wear a *kanatar* bracelet and *mutisalak* coral beads on the left wrist. The mutisalak symbolizes economic ability and social ranking. Heirloom objects include the *marangga* neck circle-pectoral and the gold jewelry called *madaka*. These objects are worn during special ceremonies but are normally kept in the attic because of their supposed strong spiritual power.

Women wear metal jewelry above the forehead, including gold or gilded *Marangga*. Their ears are decorated with *mamuli* jewelry, and golden necklaces may be worn around the neck and hang to the chest.

## Music & performance

They do describe several performance-related cultural forms: horse races, bull sacrifices, funerary rituals, and fights with spears. The *Pasola* is identified as a cultural feast of the Sumba people. In West Sumba Regency, people come from far away to watch two teams compete by throwing blunted spears at each other.

## Dance & theatre

They mention Pasola as a cultural feast involving competition between two teams throwing blunted spears, but they do not classify it as dance or theatre.

## Festivals & rituals

Sumba traditional festivals include horse races, bull sacrifices, complex funerary rituals, and fights with spears. Pasola is described as a cultural feast of the Sumba people and as a rare and distinctive cultural practice. In West Sumba Regency, people travel from far away to watch the competition, in which two teams throw blunted spears at each other.

Marapu includes ancestral worship, deity worship, customary ceremonies, and traditional places of worship called *umaratu*. Death ceremonies are among the events for which people wear especially important clothing. The sources also describe funerary rituals and the construction of megalithic tombs, most famously in Anakalang.

## Foodways

Agriculture has long been the principal occupation. Slash-and-burn agriculture is practiced in a tropical savanna climate, together with livestock keeping. Regular seasonal droughts have encouraged farmers to grow several crops simultaneously at subsistence level, including rice, beans, tuber, and corn. The traditional staple diet consists of rice and cassava. Harvests are not always abundant, but the agricultural strategy helps produce enough.

Sumba people keep cows, buffalo, chickens, sheep, and horses. Dutch missionaries and colonial officers recorded hunger as a frequent cause of military conflicts.

## Oral tradition & literature

Sumba people have a rich and relatively diverse oral folklore. A myth of origin says that the Sumba and the people of Sawu Island descend from two ancestors, Hawu Meha and Humba Meha. Hawu Meha gave birth to the Sawunese, who initially lived on Sumba Island and later migrated to the small Sawu Island, while the offspring of Humba Meha remained on Sumba.

Marapu mythology says that the first people came down through stairs from the sky to the north of the island.

## Language & religion

Kambera, also known as East Sumbanese, is a Malayo-Polynesian language spoken in the eastern half of Sumba Island. It belongs to the Bima-Sumba subgrouping within Central Malayo-Polynesian inside Malayo-Polynesian. The name Kambera comes from a traditional region near Waingapu in East Sumba Regency. Because export trades were concentrated in Waingapu in the nineteenth century, Kambera became a bridging language in eastern Sumba.

The traditional Marapu religion includes ancestral worship and deity worship and remains active in Sumba society. It is described as the philosophical center of Sumba cultural expression, including ceremonies, worship places, architecture, carvings, textiles, jewelry, and weapons. Christianity began to spread in the nineteenth century with the arrival of Christian missionaries, and the majority of Christian believers are Protestants.
